questions.enonce_markdown:
Given that the matrix $M$ is defined by

$$M = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$$

Prove by induction that

$$M^n = \begin{pmatrix} 3^n & 3^n - 2^n \\ 0 & 2^n \end{pmatrix}, \quad \text{for all } n \geq 1.$$
questions.corrige_markdown:
Let $P(n)$ be the statement $M^n = \begin{pmatrix} 3^n & 3^n - 2^n \\ 0 & 2^n \end{pmatrix}$.

**Basis, $n = 1$.** The right-hand side is $\begin{pmatrix} 3 & 3 - 2 \\ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix} = M$. So $P(1)$ is true.

**Inductive step.** Assume $P(k)$ is true for some $k \geq 1$. Then

$$M^{k+1} = M^k M = \begin{pmatrix} 3^k & 3^k - 2^k \\ 0 & 2^k \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 3^{k+1} & 3^k + 2\left(3^k - 2^k\right) \\ 0 & 2^{k+1} \end{pmatrix}.$$

The top-right entry is $3^k + 2 \cdot 3^k - 2 \cdot 2^k = 3 \cdot 3^k - 2^{k+1} = 3^{k+1} - 2^{k+1}$. Hence

$$M^{k+1} = \begin{pmatrix} 3^{k+1} & 3^{k+1} - 2^{k+1} \\ 0 & 2^{k+1} \end{pmatrix},$$

which is $P(k + 1)$.

**Conclusion.** $P(1)$ is true, and $P(k) \Rightarrow P(k + 1)$ for every $k \geq 1$. By the principle of mathematical induction, $P(n)$ is true for all integers $n \geq 1$. $\blacksquare$

questions.enonce_markdown:
A curve is given by the parametric equations

$$x = t^2, \quad y = t\left(1 - \tfrac13 t^2\right), \quad 0 \leq t \leq \sqrt3.$$

Show that the length of the curve is $2\sqrt3$.
questions.corrige_markdown:
Here $y = t - \tfrac13 t^3$, so $\dfrac{dx}{dt} = 2t$ and $\dfrac{dy}{dt} = 1 - t^2$. The arc length is $L = \displaystyle\int_0^{\sqrt3}\sqrt{\left(\frac{dx}{dt}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{dy}{dt}\right)^2}\,dt$, and

$$\left(\frac{dx}{dt}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{dy}{dt}\right)^2 = 4t^2 + (1 - t^2)^2 = 1 + 2t^2 + t^4 = (1 + t^2)^2.$$

Since $1 + t^2 > 0$, the square root is $1 + t^2$, so

$$L = \int_0^{\sqrt3}(1 + t^2)\,dt = \left[t + \frac{t^3}{3}\right]_0^{\sqrt3} = \sqrt3 + \frac{3\sqrt3}{3} = 2\sqrt3. \qquad \blacksquare$$
